sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 1! Tune projected columns k, filter threshold tau, and symbol cardinality K below. Watch zone map row groups turn green as they are pruned and see combined bandwidth saved surpass ninety-eight percent.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, look at Canvas 1! Projecting four out of one hundred columns skips ninety-six percent of bytes, and filtering above sixty skips six out of ten row groups automatically!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 1! Ten million sorted US state codes across fifty unique states occupy thirty megabytes raw and form fifty runs. Compute dictionary bit-width b, total Dictionary plus RLE compressed bytes, and overall compression ratio.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 1! Thirty megabytes of sorted state codes collapsed into fifty runs. How many bytes does Dictionary plus Run-Length Encoding actually take?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Spot on! Option B is correct. Fifty unique states require ceiling log base 2 of 50, which is 6 bits per dictionary code. Fifty runs at five bytes per run consume 250 bytes, plus 150 bytes for the dictionary page, totaling just 400 bytes—an astonishing seventy-five-thousand-fold lossless compression ratio!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Not quite. Option B is the correct answer. With fifty states, dictionary bit-width b equals six bits. Because the column is sorted into fifty runs, fifty runs times five bytes equals two hundred fifty bytes, plus one hundred fifty bytes for the state dictionary, totaling four hundred bytes and achieving a seventy-five-thousand-times compression ratio!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 2! Slide chunk size from twenty kilobytes to five hundred twelve megabytes and adjust parallel connections P below. Observe the Small-Files Collapse Cliff below one megabyte versus line-rate saturation with large shards.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, look at the throughput cliff! At twenty kilobytes, ninety-nine percent of the two-gigabyte transfer time is wasted in S3 HTTP handshakes, throttling throughput to twenty-five megabytes per second!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 2! Explain why distributed PyTorch DataLoader workers prefer reading Feather or Apache Arrow IPC files from local NVMe SSDs over Apache Parquet during high-throughput multi-GPU training loops.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 2! Why does reading ZSTD Parquet from local NVMe starve GPUs during vision training, while Arrow IPC keeps them saturated?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding mastery! Option A is correct. Parquet requires host CPU heap allocation, ZSTD decompression, and dictionary decoding on every batch, starving fast GPUs. Arrow IPC stores bytes identically to RAM layout, enabling kernel mmap zero-copy reads and direct PCIe DMA into GPU VRAM at over six gigabytes per second!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. Option A is the right answer. Parquet is optimized for archival disk savings at rest, forcing heavy CPU decompression during training. Feather and Arrow IPC eliminate CPU decoding via kernel memory mapping and direct DMA transfers to GPU memory.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 3! When streaming telemetry arrives at millions of events per second and analysts demand sub-five-minute freshness, how does Uber's Apache Hudi Merge-on-Read architecture avoid the small-files crisis?

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 3! Sub-five-minute streaming freshness without drowning S3 in millions of twenty-kilobyte Parquet files—how does Merge-on-Read solve it?

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Excellent synthesis! Option B is correct. Merge-on-Read appends incoming streaming records into append-friendly row-oriented Avro delta logs for fast freshness, while asynchronous background compaction merges those logs with columnar Parquet base files into optimal 128 to 256 megabyte chunks—cutting query planning from forty-five minutes to sub-second!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: That's not right. Option B is correct. Writing tiny Parquet files every ten seconds exhausts object store metadata. Merge-on-Read combines row-oriented Avro delta logs for rapid streaming appends with background compaction into 128-megabyte Parquet base files.
